questions.q: What row-count comparison narrows down which join is adding rows?
options: Comparing raw_customers to raw_orders
Comparing `int_orders__joined`'s count (orders-to-customers only) against `fct_orders`'s count (adds payments)
There's no useful row-count comparison available
Comparing fct_orders against itself on two different days
questions.explain: Since int_orders__joined has no payments join, a higher count on fct_orders points directly at the payments join as the source of extra rows.

questions.q: What controlled test confirms the hypothesis about `raw_payments`?
options: Querying raw_payments directly for the specific duplicated order_ids and confirming count(*) > 1 for them
Re-running dbt test with --full-refresh
Checking the Power BI refresh schedule
Rewriting the join before checking any data
questions.explain: Querying the exact suspect table for the exact suspect rows is the controlled test that confirms rather than assumes the cause.

questions.q: What real, legitimate fact about jaffle_shop orders causes `raw_payments` to have multiple rows per `order_id`?
options: A real order can be paid with more than one payment method — a split payment, e.g. part gift card, part credit card
Orders are randomly assigned extra payment rows by a nightly job
Every order always has exactly two payment rows by design
raw_payments has a bug where every row is duplicated twice
questions.explain: Split payments are a real, legitimate business scenario — not a data quality defect — that produces more than one payments row per order.

questions.q: Why does the left join in fct_orders multiply rows instead of just adding columns?
options: dbt's incremental materialization causes duplication automatically
left join always duplicates rows regardless of the data
The join condition uses the wrong column name
It matches each order row against every payments row sharing that order_id — one order paired with two payment rows produces two output rows
questions.explain: A one-to-many relationship between orders and payments means the join is a one-to-many join, not the one-to-one join it was written to be.

questions.q: Why was this bug invisible when the model was first built?
options: Most orders in the earlier, smaller dataset happened to have exactly one payment row — the fanout was rare until more split payments accumulated
It was never actually invisible — it failed immediately
Tests weren't enabled until Lesson 13
The join syntax only started being buggy after an upgrade
questions.explain: The fanout was always structurally possible but statistically rare on the smaller, earlier dataset — exactly why it surfaced only after more data accumulated.
